https://www.dw.com/en/can-the-new-pkk-la.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IeBb Although the PKK announced its dissolution a year ago, it remains unclear whether all its fighters will lay down their arms and return to Turkey Image: Sterk tv Advertisement One year ago, the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) burned its weapons in a symbolic ceremony. The move was seen as a sign of its willingness to disband. Since then, the Kurdish side has been calling on the Turkish government to take political steps. Now, parliament has passed a bill submitted by the conservative Islamic ruling party AKP and its ultranationalist ally. Officially called the "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration," it is intended to provide the legal framework for the ongoing peace process. According to official figures, 467 out of 592 MPs voted in favor of the bill. The ruling party and its ally see this as the beginning of a new era: Under certain conditions, the bill provides for a suspension of sentences for PKK members — but only after the PKK and its affiliated groups have been confirmed to have disbanded and disarmed, so that peace, brotherhood and solidarity can prevail throughout the entire country. The pro-Kurdish DEM party also supports the bill, but it views it only as a first step that must be followed by further reforms. The pro-Kurdish DEM party also voted in favor of the PKK law. At the same time, it is calling for swift political and legal reforms Image: Adem Altan/AFP PKK law divides society and parliament Fierce opposition came from the ultranationalist opposition party IYI. Even during consultations, its delegate Ayyuce Turkes, daughter of the founder of the ultranationalist and right-wing extremist Grey Wolves, accused the government of rushing a landmark bill through parliament. She also criticized what she felt was an overly conciliatory stance toward PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan. She avoided using his name, calling him a "baby killer" instead, just as government agencies and media have done for decades. There was even a physical altercation. The debate highlights just how deep the divides are within Turkish society. While the ultranationalist IYI party rejects the process, the MHP, from which the Grey Wolves emerged, is now among its most important supporters — even though it had, previously, vehemently opposed earlier peace initiatives. Observers believe this shift in course and the progress in the peace process are also a result of the changed security situation in the region. Among other things, they mention the fall of the Assad regime in Syria , the war in Gaza and the conflict between Israel, the United States and Iran . Syria and Iran are also home to large Kurdish populations that are supported by various regional actors. According to the prevailing view, a more stable relationship with the Kurds who live within Turkey's own borders could provide Ankara with more leeway in domestic and foreign policy. The justice committee of the Turkish parliament convened to discuss the draft "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration" Image: ANKA What's in the law? The law applies to convictions for PKK membership, propaganda, financing or intentional support of the organization and its structures. For prison sentences of up to 15 years, enforcement is to be suspended for five years; for longer or life sentences, the suspension is to last ten years. Ongoing investigations are to be put on hold. According to pro-government media, up to 3,600 prisoners could benefit from this. The prerequisite is the complete disbanding of the PKK and the surrender of all its weapons and ammunition. Both of these conditions have to be verified by Turkish authorities and, subsequently, officially confirmed by the National Security Council, chaired by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan . Excluded are PKK members who were convicted prior to June 1, 2005 — the date on which the current penal code came into force — as well as those convicted of homicide and whose convictions are final. That means the regulation does not apply to PKK founder Ocalan either. In February 2025, the 77-year-old had called on the PKK to disband, declared an end to the armed struggle and spoke out in favor of a political solution. Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video PKK views law as a mere first step The PKK also calls the bill a first step; it criticizes, however, wording and content. Its key demand remained unfulfilled: As long as Ocalan cannot directly coordinate the peace process under conditions of freedom, the issue of disarmament could not be resolved either. They said penal code regulations alone did not go far enough, more comprehensive democratization reforms were needed. The message was that as long as returning fighters or exiled politicians continued to be criminalized and were unable to engage in political activities legally, hardly any of them would leave the mountains where they've been staying. PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan in February 2026. The law passed by Turkey's parliament does not provide for his release from prison Image: DEM Even legal pro-Kurdish political activity has ben restricted in Turkey for decades: parties were banned, politicians were arrested or barred from political activity. To this day, elected mayors are being removed from office, and numerous politicians and activists are in prison. Among them are two former co-chairs of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP) that mainly represented Kurds, Selahattin Demirtas and Figen Yuksekdag. Peace without democratization? Political scientist Berk Esen criticizes the law for failing to offer concrete democratic solutions to the Kurdish issue. He also noted that, parallel to the peace process involving the PKK, the government had significantly increased the pressure on the largest opposition party CHP. For about two years, the Turkish judiciary has increasingly been cracking down on leading CHP politicians. Critics view this as an attempt to weaken the government party's strongest political rival. Among the most high-profile cases is that of former mayor of Istanbul and CHP presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu . He and hundreds of other party members are in prison, on charges of fraud and corruption. The entire CHP leadership under Ozgur Ozel was removed as well. He formed a new party several weeks ago. Criticism of Erdogan's role Esen primarily criticizes Erdogan's strong influence on the peace process. Although it is to be implemented by a committee chaired by the vice president and key ministers, who are also heads of the intelligence services and the National Security Council, Esen argues that it will ultimately be Erdogan as chairman of the National Security Council who decides when and which steps in the peace process will be implemented. This assessment is also shared by Reha Ruhavioglu, director of the Kurdish Studies Center. "Erdogan will clearly set the pace," Ruhavioglu said, attributing this to the asymmetric balance of power between the Turkish state and the PKK. In addition, Erdogan had learned his lessons from the failure of the peace talks between 2013 and 2015 and would now certainly assemble more control in his own hands. At the same time, experts say, Erdogan has his sights set firmly on the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections, and would want to limit any political risks associated with the process. Ruhavioglu expects further controversy, especially if former PKK fighters return to Turkey and remain at large. The government is therefore likely to allow their return, suspended sentences and political activity only gradually, and largely in response to public reaction. This article was originally written in German. Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A police officer mans a roadblock outside RAF Fairford on Sunday. Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images UK news Late-night drive and a 999 call: chance encounter that led to terrorism arrests at RAF base Local people say members of WhatsApp group noticed suspicious activity around vans in Whelford overnight Jamie Grierson and Helena Horton Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.23 EDT First published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 09.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In the early hours of Sunday morning, a resident of the village of Whelford was driving home when she saw three white vans parked on a country road. She was immediately suspicious, she said, and all the more so when she spotted a “large group of hooded and balaclavaed” men. She called 999 and police arrived on the scene 15 minutes later. The resident, who asked not to be named, told the Press Association: “It would appear that by doing so I just derailed whatever they [the men] were planning. A plucky amateur shouldn’t be spotting an unusual bit of activity at 1am when the airbase is on high alert. I think it’s absolutely astonishing.” If there had been no 999 call, it appears the authorities would have been unaware of the vans and the potential threat they posed to nearby RAF Fairford. People living in the area have been used to disturbance from protesters and a heavy police presence ever since the decision to allow the US air force to use Fairford as a base for attacks on Iran. But in recent weeks they have noticed dramatically increased security measures, with the gates of the base newly barricaded. Emergency teams deploy bomb disposal robot at RAF Fairford air base “In the prior few weeks they have put heavy, very heavy vehicles across all gates,” another resident said. She described them as “very big tractors and things like that” parked behind gates into the base, adding: “So obviously they’re taking security seriously.” The resident said “great big concrete walls” had also been placed behind some gates, including on Dunfield Loop and Whelford Road. If local people had questioned the necessity of those steps, they may have been persuaded this weekend. In the early hours of Sunday morning, others in Whelford became aware of suspicious activity as the local WhatsApp group lit up with messages. Map showing location of RAF Fairford and Whelford in the wider area One resident of Whelford, named Jason, who declined to give his surname, said they were first alerted that something was happening at about 1.30am when people in the chat group started discussing the vans. Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said the 999 call had only come after an attempt to contact the airbase itself. “Evidently, they phoned the airbase police, who didn’t answer the phone,” he said. “It just rang out, so she dialled 999.” A photograph published by the Daily Mail showed police arresting five shirtless men at night. Police later confirmed that five men had been taken into custody on suspicion of explosives and terror-related offences. Residents were then woken at 6am by police banging on their doors and telling them to leave immediately. People from 85 households were taken to a nearby leisure centre. Tudsbery said: “[The police] were banging on the door, so I went downstairs in my dressing gown. There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there’s been a major incident, said he couldn’t elaborate.” View image in fullscreen US air force military personnel tend to a Jdam precision-guided munition and a Rockwell B-1 Lancer heavy bomber on the tarmac at RAF Fairford in April. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA Thirty emergency vehicles were seen in the village, with the army, a bomb squad and counter-terrorism police all investigating at the scene. Explosives experts were seen examining three vans. The RAF base has come to prominence since March and the beginning of the US-Israeli war with Iran. From the perimeter of the RAF base it has been possible to see heavy bombs being loaded on to American aircraft. Fairford has a particularly long runway, which extends almost 2 miles (3km). It is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 and B-52, which have been deployed in attacks on Iran. The aircraft are capable of carrying large payloads, including “bunker buster” bombs. Jason, 50, was evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre at 6am on Sunday with his family and 11-week-old puppy, Poppy, and friends who were visiting from London. “We went to bed [the previous night],” he said. “It was early the next morning when the doorbell rang. It was the police asking residents to evacuate as there had been a major incident.” Jason, who works in consulting, said there were about 40 to 50 people in the leisure centre, ranging from toddlers to elderly villagers, as well as a number of dogs. He said they had been given no more details than those that had been released publicly by police. View image in fullscreen A Tesco grocery delivery vehicle is stopped at a roadblock in Fairford. Photograph: Getty Images The Fairford youth football club, about 1.5 miles north-west of Whelford, was taken over as a temporary base for the emergency service response to the incident. There were several police vehicles, ambulances, fire engines, pop-up tents and a large mobile command-unit vehicle in the grounds. It was unclear when people would be able to go back to their normal lives. Those at the leisure centre said they had been asked by authorities if they had anywhere else to stay on Sunday night. By Sunday afternoon, the cordon around the village had expanded so no one could get anywhere near it. Access to the village of Whelford remained closed. With RAF Fairford located along one side of the road, a single police vehicle acted as a blockade against further passage into the village. Tudsbery said he hoped he could get home soon. He had left his cat, Misty, behind. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/20/qata.text: In a rare public appearance, Qatar’s head of the Intelligence and Security Authority Brigadier General Khalid Mohammed Al-Nuaimi revealed how Qatar took the dramatic decision to redeploy its entire defensive systems in just six hours to counter Iran's war threats.Addressing the Global Security Forum in Doha on Tuesday, Al-Nuaimi said the redeployment was “unprecedented and successful”, based on eight months of adapting Qatar’s forces, defence capabilities, and military doctrine, which had been built for a totally different threat landscape.⁠ ⁠When asked about Qatar’s response to countering drones during the war, Qatar’s head of Intelligence replied that the six-hour overhaul was based on fast-moving changes to Qatar’s defence systems, both at concept level, but also in the allocation of defence assets.“We adapted. we redeployed and we did it within six hours,” Al-Nuaimi revealed, adding that “we were caught off guard, yet we adapted rapidly, out of sheer necessity.”Also during the Global Security Forum, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr Majed al-Ansari said the Qatar-mediated US-Iran negotiations “are ongoing and we are seeing engagement from both parties.”“The fact that we are not hearing about it is a good sign that we are doing our job properly,” the Qatari diplomat added amid the rising tensions and concerns that the Iran war may restart.Washington's fundamental shift in the Middle EastIn addressing those worrying concerns, US ambassador to Turkey and Special Presidential Envoy for Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack told the forum that "America wants a peace deal” which would be based on “ceasefire in the straits” as well as a focus on “easing the pain on the Iranian people”."Prosperity is the only answer," Barrack underlined as a way out of the current standoff, adding that "we don’t need a reboot" of the previous US-Iran peace memorandum.He identified the obstacle to a deal as a “lack of trust.”“What has happened from the beginning of these discussions and negotiations is a lack of trust," Barrack explained, which comes down to the fact that the "IRGC does not trust the US. And the US does not trust IRGC."The US envoy said he did not know if the Iran war was a mistake but admitted that it had “unintended consequences” and that US President Donald Trump is a "no forever wars president."Barrack told the forum in Qatar that the US will not leave the Middle East, even if in the region “what everybody is saying: OK, I cannot rely on America to solve all my problems,” explaining that “the bargain is not to control, but to not leave. We are not leaving.”"America is the guarantor to the world for the last 80 years and it is no longer there," the US diplomat said, explaining that "what is happening in this administration is not an abandonment, it is a message for realignment."The US envoy appeared to contradict one of the US administration’s declared goals in launching the Iran war, which was regime change in Tehran.Barrack spoke broadly about how the US pursued 23 regime changes across the Middle East and concluded that "every time we try and intervene, change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake."Instead, he said, the US’ goal is to "bring everybody, put them in a tent, give them coffee, put the guns and daggers on the table, and let’s figure something else out," through “patience, presence, dialogue."In this context, the top US diplomat also commented on the escalating tensions between Israel and Turkey, saying that "my belief is Israel is way too smart to actually pick a real fight with Turkey. I don’t think Israel wants that, I know Turkey does not want that."'Houthis are here to stay,' former MI6 chief saysMeanwhile at the forum, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr al-Ansari also reiterated his country’s position on Yemen that alongside the other Gulf nations “Qatar is supporting our brothers in Saudi Arabia in defending their sovereignty against this attack.”Also commenting on the Yemen war, the former head of the UK’s foreign intelligence agency MI6 Sir John Sawers told the Doha Global Security Forum that “the Houthis are here to stay."They are not going to be defeated, and they are going to remain in control of a large part of Yemen for the foreseeable future," Sawers said."The Houthis have got their own national Yemen agenda," he explained, adding that the group "exposed the limited options that Saudi Arabia has in terms of dealing with" them over the last 10 years, as their efforts "to sustain an alternative government (in Yemen) have not been successful over the last 10 years."
